prompt: In the stated read-heavy workload, why might a feed default to **fan-out on write** (precomputing each follower's timeline) rather than **fan-out on read**?

options.text: Because writes are far more frequent than reads.
options.explanation: Wrong. It's the other way round: feeds are read many times more often than posts are written. That imbalance is precisely why precomputing at write time pays off.

options.text: Because fan-out on read can't show posts in time order.
options.explanation: Wrong. Fan-out on read can order posts perfectly with a k-way merge by timestamp. The issue is cost and latency, not ordering.

options.text: Because reads vastly outnumber writes, so moving the merging work to the (asynchronous) write path makes the hot read path a single cache lookup.
options.explanation: Correct. You pay the fan-out cost once per post, off the user's critical path, instead of on every one of the many timeline loads.

options.text: Because fan-out on write uses less storage.
options.explanation: Wrong. Fan-out on write uses *more* storage: a post ID is copied into every follower's timeline. It trades storage and write work for read speed.

workedExample:
Compare the work per day with 500M posts, 3B timeline reads, 200 average followers and users following ~200 accounts:

```formula
push = 500M × 200 = 100B/day
pull = 3B × 200 = 600B/day
pull / push = 6
where
push: timeline appends per day with fan-out on write (posts × followers), done by background workers
pull: lookups per day with fan-out on read (timeline loads × accounts followed), done while the user waits
M: million
B: billion
day: one day; /day means per day
In words: pushing costs 100 billion background appends a day; pulling costs 600 billion lookups a day on the hot path, six times as many.
```

Pull performs 6x as many enumerated operations in this simplified model; lookups and appends do not have identical cost, all of it while a user is waiting. Push's work happens in background workers, so the timeline load is one Redis read plus hydration.

prompt: Your feed service has a user with **50 million followers** who posts 20 times a day. Your fan-out fleet sustains **1 million inserts/s** in total. Which approach should you take for this account?

options.text: Don't fan out this account's posts; at read time, fetch this account's recent posts from its (heavily cached) user timeline and merge them into each follower's precomputed timeline.
options.explanation: Correct. This is the hybrid model. Each follower pays a single extra lookup for each celebrity they follow, and that celebrity's timeline is so frequently read it's always cached.

options.text: Fan out on write like everyone else, but add more fan-out workers.
options.explanation: Wrong. Each post would need 50M inserts, ~50 s of the *entire* fleet's capacity, and 20 posts/day is 1 billion inserts from one account. When several celebrities post at once, ordinary users' feeds back up for minutes. Scaling workers treats the symptom expensively.

options.text: Switch the entire platform to fan-out on read.
options.explanation: Wrong. This fixes one account by making every timeline read expensive for every user: hundreds of lookups and a merge per load, on the hot path.

options.text: Fan out only to followers whose user IDs hash to an even number.
options.explanation: Wrong. Half the followers would never see the post. Arbitrary sampling breaks correctness; the hybrid gives everyone the post without the write amplification.

workedExample:
Cost of pushing:

```formula
t = 50M / (1M/s) = 50 s
daily = 20 × 50M = 1B
where
t: whole-fleet time to fan out one post
daily: inserts per day from this one account (20 posts a day)
M: million
B: billion
s: seconds; /s means per second
In words: each post ties up the entire fan-out fleet for 50 seconds, and the account generates a billion inserts a day on its own.
```

Cost of pulling instead:

- Each follower's timeline load adds one cached lookup (the celebrity's last ~20 posts) and a merge of a few items into a sorted list.
- The celebrity's user timeline is requested millions of times, so it stays hot in cache.

So set a threshold (e.g. > 1M followers) above which accounts are pulled, not pushed.

prompt: A celebrity with 40M followers posts, and fan-out takes several minutes. A follower near the front of the list replies within seconds, and the reply is fanned out to mutual followers *before* the original reaches them. They see the reply before the post it answers. What's the best structural fix?

options.text: Make the reply's fan-out wait until the celebrity's fan-out has finished.
options.explanation: Wrong. Cross-post dependencies in the fan-out pipeline would be complex and fragile, and would delay replies by minutes.

options.text: Use the hybrid model: don't fan out the celebrity's posts; merge them in at read time from their cached user timeline, so everyone sees the original as soon as it exists.
options.explanation: Correct. With pull for huge accounts, pull avoids the bulk fan-out delay, but stale source/cache reads and partial failures can still hide the parent. If causal presentation is required, fetch or defer replies whose parent is unavailable.

options.text: Sort each timeline by post ID before returning it.
options.explanation: Partly helps ordering within a timeline, but it can't show a post that hasn't arrived in that timeline yet. The reply still appears without its parent.

options.text: Add more fan-out workers so the celebrity's fan-out completes in under 5 seconds.
options.explanation: Wrong as the main fix. 40M inserts in 5 s means 8M inserts/s just for one post, many times a normal fleet's capacity, and the race returns as soon as several celebrities post together.

workedExample:
The race exists because one post's delivery is spread over minutes:

```
at 0 s     celebrity posts
at 5 s    follower A gets it, replies
at 10 s   reply fanned out to B
at 3 min  original finally reaches B
```

With pull for huge accounts, B's read at 10 s can merge the original from the celebrity's user timeline without waiting for bulk fan-out, provided that read sees the committed post. Stale caches or failed lookups still need parent fetching or deferral. Do not infer causality from Snowflake IDs under clock skew; use the reply-parent relationship if parent-before-reply display is required.
